past_medical_history: Eclampsia during first pregnancy (3 years ago)

patient.chief_complaint: Severe headache 2 hours postpartum, visual disturbances, seizure reported by nursing staff
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Kelly is a 35-year-old woman with a history of eclampsia in her first pregnancy who delivered her second child by vaginal delivery 2 hours ago. Delivery was unremarkable with a maximum systolic BP of 148 mmHg intrapartum. Two hours post-delivery, nursing staff noted she was confused and called for help. The patient reports a severe sudden headache that began approximately 30 minutes after delivery, initially attributed to post-delivery discomfort. She had one witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 45 seconds. Blood pressure at the time of seizure was 182/110 mmHg. She was given magnesium sulfate IV (loading dose) for presumed eclampsia given her history. However, the neurology team is concerned because: 1) the headache onset was sudden (thunderclap quality), 2) the post-delivery period is a known high-risk period for SAH from cerebrovascular events, and 3) CT is required. She currently has severe headache 8/10, photophobia, and neck stiffness 2 hours after the seizure. Her BP remains elevated despite magnesium.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4; GCS 15; mild post-ictal drowsiness recovering; photophobic; BP still 176/106
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: PERRL 4mm; blurring of vision reported - mild bilateral papilledema on fundoscopy (hypertensive); EOM intact
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric; brisk but not hyperreflexic; plantars flexor
neurological_exam.additional: Mild nuchal rigidity; Kernig equivocal; clinical picture consistent with either eclampsia or SAH - workup required

findings.location: Basal cisterns and bilateral Sylvian fissures
findings.description: Moderate hyperdense subarachnoid blood in basal cisterns - not typical for eclampsia pattern
Subtle cortical hypodensity posterior regions - possible PRES component

additional_observations: Fisher grade 3 SAH in a postpartum patient - this is NOT eclampsia alone
PRES changes visible posteriorly - can co-occur with SAH in postpartum hypertension
ct.impression: Moderate subarachnoid hemorrhage (Fisher grade 3) in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures. Superimposed posterior cortical changes consistent with PRES (posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome) from hypertension. In postpartum setting with prior eclampsia history, eclampsia is an important differential, but CT confirms SAH that requires CTA and aneurysm workup. CTA urgently required.
recommended_actions: Continue magnesium sulfate for eclampsia seizure prophylaxis

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: WBC 16.8 x10^9/L (H), Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL (L), Platelets 142 x10^9/L (L), Sodium 132 mEq/L (L), Glucose 142 mg/dL (H), LDH 342 U/L (H), AST 68 U/L (H), Troponin I 0.16 ng/mL (H).

findings: Note: magnesium IV can affect ECG
ecg.interpretation: Neurogenic T-wave inversions and QTc prolongation. Note: IV magnesium can cause AV block and QTc prolongation at toxic levels - monitor magnesium levels.

output.tracer_or_protocol: IV contrast CTA (radiation exposure discussed with patient post-delivery)

findings.finding: Small irregular aneurysm 4.2 x 3.8 mm with daughter sac - likely ruptured

output.impression: Right MCA bifurcation aneurysm 4.2 mm with daughter sac, consistent with ruptured aneurysm in postpartum patient. No RCVS pattern. DSA for treatment. Urgent treatment required.

findings.location: Bilateral occipital, parietal, posterior temporal regions

signal_characteristics.FLAIR: Bilateral posterior white matter FLAIR hyperintensity - vasogenic edema

output.impression: MRI shows both PRES (posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome) from hypertension/eclampsia AND subarachnoid hemorrhage. Both diagnoses are present simultaneously. PRES is managed with BP control (already doing for SAH) and seizure management (magnesium). Clinical correlation recommended.

output.proposed: Continue magnesium sulfate IV maintenance (2 g/hr) for eclampsia prophylaxis
interactions: Magnesium + nimodipine: magnesium blocks calcium channels - additive calcium channel blockade, monitor BP and neuromuscular function
warnings: Respiratory depression risk at toxic levels (>12 mEq/L)
Loss of patellar reflex at 7-10 mEq/L - check before each dose
Calcium gluconate at bedside as antidote
alternatives: Levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis if magnesium not tolerated (limited obstetric evidence)

output.impression: Borderline right MCA vasospasm correlating with right MCA aneurysm. Close monitoring. Nimodipine and euvolemia.
recommended_actions: Continue nimodipine with monitoring re: magnesium interaction

output.query: Postpartum subarachnoid hemorrhage eclampsia RCVS differential diagnosis

results.finding: SAH in postpartum period: aneurysmal SAH, RCVS-associated SAH, eclampsia overlap
CTA mandatory in postpartum severe headache - CT and CTA, not just eclampsia management
RCVS can cause convexity SAH without aneurysm - CTA shows beading not saccular aneurysm
Aneurysmal SAH in pregnancy: treat aneurysm regardless of postpartum state

output.summary: Postpartum severe headache requires SAH workup even with eclampsia history. This case shows co-occurrence of eclampsia/PRES and aneurysmal SAH. RCVS must be differentiated (angiographic beading vs saccular aneurysm on CTA). Aneurysmal SAH requires definitive treatment regardless of obstetric status.

output.impression: Mild Takotsubo cardiomyopathy in postpartum SAH. EF 54%. Peripartum cardiomyopathy also possible in differential - serial echo and cardiology consult recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage in postpartum period with co-existing eclampsia and PRES

differential.key_features: CT and CSF confirm SAH; aneurysm on CTA - SAH co-exists with eclampsia
CTA shows saccular aneurysm not beading pattern; distribution is basal cistern not convexity
Echo shows mild Takotsubo; serial echo needed; neurogenic vs peripartum difficult to distinguish

optimal_actions.action: CT head - do not assume eclampsia alone; confirm SAH
optimal_actions.expected_finding: SAH in basal cisterns + PRES changes - SAH co-existing with eclampsia
Saccular right MCA aneurysm (not RCVS beading)
Additive calcium channel blockade - monitor BP and Mg levels

optimal_actions.action: Literature search - postpartum SAH eclampsia overlap
optimal_actions.expected_finding: SAH and eclampsia can co-exist; CT/CTA mandatory in postpartum severe headache
PRES + SAH both confirmed on MRI

critical_actions: Do not attribute all symptoms to eclampsia - SAH must be excluded with CT and LP
CTA to identify aneurysm and differentiate from RCVS
Continue magnesium for eclampsia; add nimodipine for SAH vasospasm prophylaxis
BP control serves both eclampsia/PRES and SAH management
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose eclampsia alone without CT and LP in postpartum thunderclap headache
Do not withhold CT from postpartum patient with thunderclap headache
Do not give sumatriptan (often used for postpartum headache) in confirmed SAH
key_reasoning_points: SAH and eclampsia/PRES can co-exist in postpartum patients - thunderclap headache always requires imaging
CTA differentiates aneurysmal SAH from RCVS: saccular aneurysm (SAH) vs arterial beading (RCVS)
Prior eclampsia history is a red herring - increases pre-test probability for eclampsia but does not exclude SAH
Magnesium sulfate blocks calcium channels - additive effect with nimodipine, monitor closely
HELLP syndrome component (elevated LDH, AST, borderline platelets) adds complexity to management
Postpartum period is a high-risk time for both SAH (aneurysm) and RCVS

red_herrings.data_point: Prior eclampsia history and eclampsia diagnosis in current pregnancy
red_herrings.intended_effect: Lead clinician to attribute all symptoms to eclampsia and skip SAH workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Eclampsia and SAH can co-exist; thunderclap headache requires CT and CTA regardless of eclampsia diagnosis
